definition: The steady tick you feel under a piece of music, like a clock or a heartbeat. It is what your foot taps to, and it carries on even when the tune holds a long note.
One tick of the [[pulse|pulse]]. Notes are measured in beats: a note can last 1 beat, 2 beats, or more.
A note with a filled-in head and a stem with no hook. In 4/4 it lasts 1 beat, twice as long as a [[quaver|quaver]].
A note with a hollow head and a stem. It lasts twice as long as a [[crotchet|crotchet]]: 2 beats in the music you meet first.
One of the equal boxes that music is divided into. Every [[bar|bar]] in a piece normally holds the same number of beats.
The upright line drawn across the music where one [[bar|bar]] ends and the next begins.
A note with a hollow head and no stem. It lasts 4 [[beat|beats]], so in 4/4 time it fills a whole [[bar|bar]].
A note with a filled-in head and a stem with one hook. It lasts half as long as a [[crotchet|crotchet]]: half a [[beat|beat]].
A note with a filled-in head and a stem with two hooks. It lasts half as long as one [[quaver|quaver]]: a quarter of a [[beat|beat]].
A symbol that shows silence: a moment when you do not play. Each rest lasts as long as the matching note, such as a [[crotchet|crotchet]].
A rest that lasts 4 [[beat|beats]], or a whole silent [[bar|bar]] in any time. It hangs below the fourth [[line|line]] from the bottom.
A rest that lasts 2 [[beat|beats]]. It sits on top of the middle [[line|line]] of the [[stave|stave]].
A rest that lasts 1 [[beat|beat]]. It looks like a zigzag, sitting around the middle of the [[stave|stave]].
A rest that lasts half a [[beat|beat]]. It has a curly, hook-like shape with a round blob at the top.
A rest that lasts a quarter of a [[beat|beat]]. It looks like one [[quaver-rest|quaver rest]] with an extra hook.
A note with a dot after its head. The dot adds half the note's own length: a dotted [[crotchet|crotchet]] lasts 1 and a half [[beat|beats]].
A curved line joining two notes of the same [[pitch|pitch]]. Play the first note and hold it for both lengths, without playing the second.
Two numbers at the start of the music, such as 3/4. The top number counts the [[beat|beats]] in each [[bar|bar]]; the bottom says which note gets one beat.
Time in which each [[beat|beat]] splits into two equal parts, such as 2/4, 3/4 or 4/4.
Time with two [[beat|beats]] in each [[bar|bar]], such as 2/4. The first beat is strong and the second is weak.
Time with three [[beat|beats]] in each [[bar|bar]], such as 3/4. The first beat is strong; the other two are weak.
Time with four [[beat|beats]] in each [[bar|bar]], such as 4/4. Beats 1 and 3 are stronger than beats 2 and 4.
A thick line that joins [[quaver|quavers]] or [[semiquaver|semiquavers]] into a group, instead of separate hooks.
A symbol at the start of the [[stave|stave]] for higher notes. Its curl wraps around the G line, so it is also called the G [[clef|clef]].
A symbol at the start of the [[stave|stave]] for lower notes. Its two dots surround the F line, so it is also called the F [[clef|clef]].
A symbol at the start of the [[stave|stave]] that fixes the names of the [[line|lines]] and [[space|spaces]].
A short extra line above or below the [[stave|stave]]. Notes too high or too low for the stave sit on or between these lines.
The symbol ♯ that raises a note by one [[semitone|semitone]]: the next note up on the [[keyboard|keyboard]].
The symbol ♭ that lowers a note by one [[semitone|semitone]]: the next note down on the [[keyboard|keyboard]].
The symbol ♮ that cancels a [[sharp|sharp]] or [[flat|flat]]. The note goes back to its original, unaltered pitch.
A [[sharp|sharp]], [[flat|flat]] or [[natural|natural]] written beside a note. It applies to that note for the rest of the [[bar|bar]].
The smallest step on the [[keyboard|keyboard]], from one note to the very next, black or white.
A step on the [[keyboard|keyboard]] made of two [[semitone|semitones]], such as from C to D. It skips one note in between.
A row of [[note|notes]] in pitch order, from one note up to the same note an [[octave|octave]] higher. Each scale follows its own pattern of [[tone|tones]] and [[semitone|semitones]].
A [[scale|scale]] with the pattern [[tone|tone]], [[tone|tone]], [[semitone|semitone]], [[tone|tone]], [[tone|tone]], [[tone|tone]], [[semitone|semitone]]. It often sounds bright and happy.
The set of notes a piece is built on, centred on one main note: its [[tonic|tonic]].
The [[sharp|sharps]] or [[flat|flats]] written at the start of each [[stave|stave]], after the [[clef|clef]]. They show the [[key|key]] of the piece.
The first and most important note of a [[scale|scale]] or [[key|key]]. Music often comes to rest on it.
A note's position in a [[scale|scale]], counted up from the [[tonic|tonic]] as 1, 2, 3 and so on.
The distance between two [[note|notes]], counted in [[note-name|letter names]]. Count from the lower note up to the higher, including both. C up to E is a [[3rd|third]].
The interval covering two [[note-name|letter names]], such as C up to D. It is usually a [[tone|tone]] or a [[semitone|semitone]].
The interval covering three [[note-name|letter names]], such as C up to E. Stacked thirds build many [[chord|chords]].
The interval covering four [[note-name|letter names]], such as C up to F.
The interval covering five [[note-name|letter names]], such as C up to G.
The interval covering six [[note-name|letter names]], such as C up to A.
The interval covering seven [[note-name|letter names]], such as C up to B.
The interval covering eight [[note-name|letter names]], such as C up to the next C. It is the [[octave|octave]].
A [[chord|chord]] of three notes stacked in [[3rd|thirds]]. It has a bottom note, a third above it, and another third above that.
The [[triad|triad]] built on the [[tonic|tonic]] of a [[key|key]], such as C, E and G in C major. It sounds settled and at home.
Two or more [[note|notes]] played together. Chords give music its harmony.
Slow and calm.
Quick and lively.
Quite quick, but slower than allegro.
At a walking pace.
At a moderate speed.
Slow.
Gradually getting faster (accel.).
Gradually getting slower (rit.).
Gradually getting slower, and often broader (rall.).
Return to the original speed.
Gradually getting louder (cresc.).
Gradually getting quieter (decresc.).
Gradually getting quieter (dim.). It means the same as decrescendo.
How loud or quiet music is played. Signs such as [[forte|forte]] and [[piano|piano]] show it.
The wedge signs that open for getting louder and close for getting quieter. They mean the same as [[crescendo|crescendo]] and [[decrescendo|decrescendo]].
Loud (f).
Very loud (ff).
Moderately loud (mf).
Moderately quiet (mp).
Quiet (p).
Very quiet (pp).
In a singing style.
Sweet and soft.
Smooth and connected, with no gaps between notes.
Short and detached, with a gap after each note.
Go back to the beginning (D.C.).
Go back to the sign (D.S.).
Play on to the end, marked [[fine|Fine]].
The end: where the piece stops.
A little.
Very much.
Half, or medium.
A curved line over or under notes that tells you to play them smoothly, as [[legato|legato]]. Unlike a [[tie|tie]], it joins notes of different pitch.
A sideways V mark that tells you to play that note louder. It asks for more force than the notes around it.
A sign over a [[note|note]] or [[rest|rest]] that tells you to hold it for longer than its normal length.
Signs that tell you to play a section again. A double [[bar-line|bar line]] with dots marks the start or end of the section.
A marking such as ♩ = 80 that tells you how many [[beat|beats]] to play each minute. The note symbol shows which note counts as one beat.
